easy.heading: Warming Up With Some Simple Math
easy.body:
Today’s easy puzzle was a lovely way to wake up the brain. I started by looking for the most restrictive spots, and that sum target of 2 at cell [0,4] jumped out at me immediately. Since it was paired with cell [1,4], which had to be less than 4, I looked at my dominoes and realized the [2,3] domino was the perfect fit. Putting the 2 in the sum spot and the 3 in the less-than spot worked like a charm.

From there, I noticed the equal signs. Cells [1,1] and [1,2] had to match, as did [1,3] and [2,3]. Since I had already used the 3, I tried the [5,5] double domino for the [1,3] and [2,3] pair, which made them both 5. That left me with a few more spots to fill, including a greater-than-4 constraint at [0,0]. Using the [3,5] domino there, with the 5 sitting on the constraint, felt like the right move to wrap things up quickly.

medium.heading: Connecting the Dots in the Middle
medium.body:
The medium puzzle felt like a big logic chain today. The breakthrough for me was the sequence of equal constraints. I saw that [0,2] had to equal [1,2], and [2,2] had to equal [2,3], which also had to match up with [1,3] and [1,4]. It felt like a row of falling dominoes! I started at [2,1], which had a sum target of 0. That’s a huge hint because only a 0 can go there. I used the [2,0] domino, putting the 0 at [2,1] and the 2 at [1,1].

Once [1,1] was a 2, the sum target of 7 for [0,1] and [1,1] meant [0,1] had to be a 5. I paired that with the 1 from the [5,1] domino in the empty cell at [0,0]. The rest of the puzzle fell into place once I used the [3,3] domino for the [0,2] and [1,2] equality. It’s all about finding that one anchor point, like that zero, and letting the math lead you the rest of the way.

hard.heading: Navigating the Unequal Maze
hard.body:
Wow, Rodolfo Kurchan really put us to the test with this hard grid! The biggest challenge was definitely the unequal region involving [2,3], [2,4], [3,3], and [4,3]. Having four different cells that all have to be unique while also satisfying nearby sums is a lot to juggle. I spent a long time staring at the bottom right, where [3,6] and [4,6] had to sum to 2. I eventually settled on using a 0 and 2 there, which helped me figure out the sum of 10 for [2,5] and [2,6].

The real breakthrough happened when I looked at the sum of 8 for [3,1] and [3,2]. By testing out the [4,2] and [6,5] dominoes in that area, I finally managed to satisfy the unequal constraint in the center. I had to backtrack once when I realized I’d used the same value twice in the unequal zone, but once I swapped the [4,5] domino into the [2,4] and [2,5] position, everything clicked. It was a tough nut to crack, but so satisfying to finish!

explanation.tips: Always start with the smallest or largest sum targets, as they usually have the fewest possible domino combinations. If you see a zero or a double domino, use those as anchors to build out the rest of your solution. Don't forget to cross off your dominoes as you place them so you don't accidentally use the same one twice!
explanation.learned: I learned that equal constraints are actually much more helpful than they look because they act like bridges between different regions. If you know the value of one cell, the bridge tells you the value of the next one instantly. Today also reminded me that sum targets in single-cell regions are basically free gifts—they tell you exactly what pip value needs to go in that spot without any guessing.

faqs.question: What is the goal of the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: The goal is to place a set of standard dominoes onto a grid so that every cell is filled and all mathematical constraints, like sums and equalities, are satisfied.

faqs.question: How do sum constraints work in Pips?
faqs.answer: A sum constraint indicates that the pip values within that specific colored region must add up to the target number shown in the corner of the region.

faqs.question: What does the unequal constraint mean?
faqs.answer: An unequal constraint means that every cell within that highlighted region must contain a different pip value; no numbers can be repeated inside that area.

faqs.question: Can I use the same domino more than once?
faqs.answer: No, you are provided with a specific set of unique dominoes for each puzzle, and each one can only be placed on the grid once.

faqs.question: What should I do if I get stuck on a hard Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Look for cells with very low sum targets or regions with equality symbols. These often limit the possible dominoes you can use and provide a starting point for the rest of the grid.
